title: JavaScript closures: functions that remember

authoring.author: Parikshaa content team
authoring.originality: Written for Parikshaa: our own lesson text and examples on javascript closures: functions that remember, examples, code, quiz and explanations; no text from any site, book or course.

outcomes: can explain what a closure captures and how long it lives
can use a closure to keep private state per instance
can predict var versus let behaviour in loops that create functions

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.body: Closures are everywhere in JavaScript: every event handler, every callback, every React hook depends on them. "What is a closure?" and "what does this loop print?" are among the most asked front-end interview questions, and the bugs they cause (the wrong value in a callback, state shared by accident) are some of the hardest to see.

sections.heading: A function plus the variables it can see
sections.body:
When a function is created inside another function, it can use the outer function's variables. A **closure** is that inner function **together with the variables it refers to**. The surprising part: those variables **stay alive after the outer function returns**, for as long as the inner function exists.

In `makeDispenser(prefix)`, the variable `next` is created when `makeDispenser` runs. The returned function uses `next`, so JavaScript keeps it. Each call to `makeDispenser` creates a **new** `next`, so two dispensers count independently.

This gives JavaScript **private state** without classes: nothing outside can read or change `next`; only the returned function can.

> **Note:** A closure captures **variables, not values**. If the variable changes later, the function sees the new value. This one sentence explains the loop puzzle below.

sections.heading: The loop puzzle: var versus let
sections.body:
A `var` variable belongs to the **whole function** (or the whole script), not to the loop body. A loop with `var i` has **one** `i`, and every function created in the loop closes over that same variable. When the functions finally run, the loop has finished and `i` is 4, one past the last value, so all of them return 4.

`let` and `const` are **block-scoped**, and a `for (let j ...)` loop creates a **fresh `j` for every iteration**. Each function closes over its own `j`, so they return 1, 2, 3.

Before `let` existed, people fixed this with an immediately invoked function that took `i` as a parameter, creating a new variable per iteration. Today, `let` is the fix: **use `let` or `const`, never `var`, in new code**.

sections.heading: Planning the hands-on task
sections.body:
The task gives every queue its own token numbers: the input names counters, and each request prints the next token for that counter. The starter keeps `next` at the top of the file, **outside** `makeDispenser`, so all dispensers share one counter: requests `C, L, C` print `C1, L2, C3` instead of `C1, L1, C2`.

The fix is to move `let next = 1;` **inside** `makeDispenser`. Now each call to `makeDispenser` creates a new `next`, and the arrow function it returns closes over that one.

Trace the first test, `C L C L L`: the program creates the C dispenser on the first request (`C1`), the L dispenser on the second (`L1`), then C again (`C2`, its own `next` is now 2), L (`L2`), L (`L3`). The dictionary `dispensers` stores one closure per counter name, so each name always reaches the same closure and its counter.

This is the same pattern behind module-level private state, memoised functions, and React's `useState`: **a function that returns another function is a factory for independent pieces of state.**

sections.heading: Closures you already use
sections.body:
Once you know the idea, you will see closures in most JavaScript you read:

- **Event handlers.** `button.addEventListener("click", () => save(studentId))` closes over `studentId`. When the click happens minutes later, the handler still knows which student it was made for.
- **Callbacks with settings.** `const byFee = (limit) => (hostel) => hostel.fee <= limit;` returns a filter that remembers `limit`: `hostels.filter(byFee(5000))`.
- **Memoisation.** A function can keep a `cache` object in its closure and return stored answers for repeated inputs, without exposing the cache to anyone.
- **React hooks.** Each render's event handlers close over that render's state. The well-known "stale state" bug, where a timer keeps seeing an old value, is a closure capturing the variable from an earlier render.

The question to ask when such code misbehaves is always the same: **which variable did this function capture, and has it changed since?**

sections.heading: Common mix-ups
sections.body:
**Many students think a closure copies the variable's value when the function is created.** It keeps a reference to the variable itself; later changes are visible.

**Many students think closures are a special syntax.** Every function in JavaScript is a closure over the scope it was created in; you notice it only when the function outlives that scope.

**Many students think closures leak memory.** A closure keeps its variables alive only while the function is reachable. Problems come from keeping functions around (for example, event listeners never removed), not from closures themselves.

sections.heading: Interview questions
sections.body: Answers as a strong candidate would say them.

qa.a: A function together with the variables from the scope where it was created. Those variables stay alive as long as the function does, even after the outer function has returned, which lets the function keep private state.

qa.q: Why does a var loop that pushes `() => i` give 4, 4, 4?
qa.a: var is function-scoped, so the loop has one i shared by all the functions, and closures capture the variable, not its value. By the time the functions run, the loop has set i to 4. With let, each iteration gets its own binding, so they return 1, 2, 3.

qa.q: How do you make private state in JavaScript without a class?
qa.a: Return functions from a factory function. The variables declared in the factory are reachable only through the returned functions, like the counter inside makeDispenser.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
- A closure is a function plus the variables of the scope it was created in.
- Captured variables live as long as the function does.
- Closures capture variables, not values.
- `var` gives one variable per function; `let` gives one per loop iteration.
- A factory function returning closures creates independent private state.

quiz.stem: `const a = makeDispenser('A'); const b = makeDispenser('B'); a(); b(); a();` What does the last call return?
quiz.explanation: a has its own next; it was used once before, so this call returns A2.

quiz.stem: `for (var k = 0; k < 2; k++) setTimeout(() => console.log(k));` What prints?
quiz.explanation: One shared k, which is 2 when the callbacks run.
It keeps references to the variables, so later changes are visible.

quiz.stem: Which change makes the var loop print 0 then 1?
options: Use const instead of var for k
quiz.explanation: let creates a new binding per iteration; const would fail because k++ reassigns it.

revision_card.front: Closures in one line, the var-in-a-loop bug, and the private-state pattern?
revision_card.back: A function plus the variables of its creation scope, kept alive with it; captures variables, not values. var loop: one shared variable (use let). Factory returning functions = private state per instance.
